diagrams.caption: Pulse inverse construction: the original pulse schedule (left) is inverted by negating amplitudes and reversing time ordering to create the pulse inverse (right).

Adaptive KIK workflow: the circuits K(K_I K)^m are executed for m = 0, 1, ..., M and their expectation values are combined with coefficients a_m fixed analytically by a single measured noise-strength parameter.

description: Adaptive KIK mitigates errors using pulse-based inverse evolutions. If K denotes the noisy implementation of a target unitary U, and K_I denotes a noisy inverse evolution generated by reversing the drive in time and negating it, H_I(t) = -H(T-t), then to first order in the Magnus expansion both pick up the same accumulated noise. That gives the KIK formula \(U \approx K(K_I K)^{-1/2}\): the noise channel is reconstructed from the folded circuit and divided out, rather than extrapolated away.

The inverse matters. Constructing K_I at the pulse level, rather than reusing a gate as its own inverse the way circuit folding does, is what makes the noise in K_I match the noise in K. In a CNOT calibration experiment, folding-based ZNE, which uses the CNOT as its own inverse, gives erroneous and inconsistent results where KIK succeeds.

Since \((K_I K)^{-1/2}\) is not directly implementable, it is approximated by a polynomial in \(K_I K\), so the protocol executes the circuits \(K(K_I K)^m\) for m = 0, 1, ..., M and combines their outcomes linearly. The coefficients are optimized analytically from a single experimental parameter that probes the noise strength, which is the adaptive part: no tomography, no noise learning, and no machine learning stage. The number of distinct circuits is independent of system size.

The only assumption on the noise is time locality, so spatially correlated, time-dependent and gate-dependent noise are all covered, and drifts over the course of long experiments can be suppressed by choosing the execution order of the circuits appropriately. Combined with randomized compiling, the method handles coherent errors as well. Layered KIK amplifies noise layer by layer instead of globally, which removes the incompatibility with mid-circuit measurements and dynamic circuits and cuts the residual error from unaccounted high-order Magnus terms.
how_it_works: Optionally apply randomized compiling to the target circuit to convert coherent errors into stochastic Pauli noise.
Construct the inverse evolution K_I from the inverse driving \(H_I(t) = -H(T-t)\): negate the pulse amplitudes and reverse their time ordering. In the noiseless limit this implements \(U^\dagger\).
Execute the circuits \(K(K_I K)^m\) for \(m = 0, 1, \ldots, M\) and measure the expectation value \(\langle A \rangle_m\) for each.
Measure the single parameter that probes the noise strength, and use it to fix the coefficients \(a_m^{(M)}\) of the polynomial expansion of \((K_I K)^{-1/2}\).
Combine the measured values as \(\langle A \rangle^{(M)} = \sum_m a_m^{(M)} \langle A \rangle_m\).
Interleave the execution order of the different circuits so that slow drifts in the noise affect all of them equally.

advantages: Handles moderate-to-strong noise where circuit-folding ZNE fails
No tomography, noise learning, or machine learning stage required
Number of distinct circuits is independent of system size
Bias is suppressed exponentially in the expansion order M when the noise is below a threshold, unlike ZNE which offers no accuracy guarantee
Covers spatially correlated, time-dependent and gate-dependent noise; only time locality is assumed
Resilient to noise drift over experiments lasting days, given a suitable execution order
Integrates with randomized compiling to handle coherent errors
disadvantages: Requires the ability to construct the proper inverse evolution, which generally means pulse-level control rather than reusing a gate as its own inverse
Rests on truncating the Magnus expansion at first order; high-order Magnus terms leave a residual error, which is what Layered KIK addresses
The time-locality assumption on the noise fails under pronounced non-Markovian noise
Global noise amplification in the original formulation is incompatible with mid-circuit measurements and dynamic circuits
Variance grows with the expansion order, as with any linear combination of noisy estimates
use_cases: Near-term algorithms on superconducting processors with pulse-level access
Long-duration experiments where noise drifts between calibrations
Circuits with spatially correlated noise or crosstalk
Gate calibration, where a noise-induced bias in the calibration measurement produces coherent errors
Moderate-to-strong noise regimes where ZNE folding is insufficient
Dynamic circuits and quantum error correction experiments (Layered KIK variant)
